articles.headline: OFAC Amends Venezuela-Related General License, Issues New FAQ
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced the issuance of an amended Venezuela-related General License (GL) and a new Frequently Asked Question (FAQ) on October 16, 2026. This action updates existing guidance concerning transactions involving Venezuela.

The specific details of the amendments and the new FAQ were not immediately released, but such updates typically clarify the scope of authorized activities or provide additional guidance on compliance with Venezuela sanctions programs. These changes often reflect evolving U.S. policy towards the Venezuelan government and its state-owned entities.

Stakeholders involved in Venezuela-related transactions are advised to review the updated GL and FAQ to ensure ongoing compliance and understand any new permissions or restrictions. OFAC regularly adjusts its sanctions programs in response to geopolitical developments.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iranian and Cuban Entities, Issues New and Amended General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations and a Cuba designation on October 15, 2026. Concurrently, OFAC issued new and amended General Licenses (GLs) and Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) to provide guidance on these actions.

The Treasury Department stated that these new Iran sanctions were enacted under 'Operation Economic Outcast,' targeting offshore banks affiliated with Bank Mellat and Bank Shahr, an Iraqi bank, and a network involved in Iranian oil sales, aiming to sever the Islamic Republic's access to foreign currency and international banking networks. The Cuba designation targeted Banco Internacional de Comercio S.A. (BICSA) for providing services to Iran's Karafarin Bank, which was sanctioned in 2020.

The new and amended GLs and FAQs are intended to clarify the scope of permissible activities following these designations. Foreign financial institutions are particularly warned that engaging with sanctioned Iranian financial institutions could lead to sanctions without prior notification.

articles.headline: U.S. Lifts Sanctions on Venezuela's National Assembly President Jorge Rodriguez
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced the removal of Jorge Rodriguez, the head of Venezuela's National Assembly, from its Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) blacklist on October 14, 2026. This action reverses sanctions that were initially imposed during the first Trump administration.

Rodriguez, who has served as president of the National Assembly since 2021, is the brother of Venezuela's interim President Delcy Rodriguez. His delisting is seen as a significant step in warming relations between Washington and Caracas, following recent U.S.-Venezuela energy pacts and ongoing diplomatic talks.

This move follows previous sanctions easements on Delcy Rodriguez, Venezuela's central bank, and its state-owned airline, signaling a shift in U.S. policy from economic pressure to negotiation. The decision is reportedly linked to a deal granting the U.S. access to 17 Venezuelan oil fields and efforts to open up the country's energy industry to foreign companies.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations related to counter narcotics and counter terrorism efforts on October 13, 2026. These actions target individuals and entities involved in illicit activities that threaten U.S. national security.

While specific details of the designated parties were not immediately available, such designations typically involve asset freezes and prohibitions on transactions with U.S. persons. These measures aim to disrupt the financial networks of criminal organizations and terrorist groups.

These designations underscore the U.S. government's ongoing commitment to combating international drug trafficking and terrorism through financial sanctions. Affected parties are advised to consult OFAC's updated Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) List for more information.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces Settlement with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics, Designates ICC Official, and Removes Burma Designation
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a settlement agreement with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics on October 9, 2026, for sanctions violations. Concurrently, OFAC issued a designation related to the International Criminal Court (ICC) and associated General Licenses, and removed a Burma-related designation.

The settlement with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics addresses alleged violations of OFAC sanctions regulations, highlighting the agency's continued enforcement efforts against companies failing to comply with U.S. sanctions laws. The specific terms of the settlement were detailed in a separate enforcement action.

The ICC designation and accompanying General Licenses indicate a targeted approach to specific individuals or entities associated with the court, while the removal of a Burma-related designation suggests a reassessment of sanctions policy concerning that country.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Russia-Related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued a new Russia-related General License (GL) on October 9, 2026. This action provides specific authorizations for certain transactions that would otherwise be prohibited under existing Russia sanctions programs.

The new GL, numbered 135, specifically concerns specified activities involving Russian-origin diesel fuel. This authorization aims to address particular economic or humanitarian considerations while maintaining the broader sanctions framework against Russia.

Entities engaged in transactions related to Russian-origin diesel fuel should carefully review the terms and conditions of this new General License to ensure compliance. This issuance reflects OFAC's dynamic approach to managing sanctions in response to evolving market and geopolitical factors.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Iran-Related Designations, Amends Russia-Related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on October 8, 2026, alongside the issuance of an Iran-related General License and an amended Russia-related General License. These actions reflect ongoing efforts to address threats from both Iran and Russia.

The Iran-related designations target entities and individuals deemed to be supporting the Iranian regime's illicit activities, while the new Iran-related General License may provide specific carve-outs for certain humanitarian or other authorized transactions. These measures are part of a broader strategy to exert economic pressure on Iran.

The amended Russia-related General License indicates adjustments to existing sanctions against Russia, potentially clarifying or modifying permissible activities. All parties involved in transactions with Iran or Russia are advised to review these updates to ensure compliance with the evolving sanctions landscape.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Iran-Related Alert, Designations Removals and Updates
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced designations removals and updates on October 5, 2026, and published an Iran-related OFAC Alert along with an amended Iran-related Frequently Asked Question (FAQ). These actions are part of 'Operation Economic Outcast,' aimed at cutting off financial resources for the Iranian regime.

The OFAC Alert specifically warns foreign financial institutions that continued business with Iran or its financial sector could lead to sanctions without advance notification. This alert also removed previous language suggesting OFAC would generally contact an FFI before finding it engaged in sanctionable activity.

The designations removals and updates reflect ongoing adjustments to the sanctions list, while the amended FAQ provides further clarification on Iran-related compliance. Foreign financial institutions are urged to take immediate action to terminate any activities and relationships with sanctioned Iranian financial institutions.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new counter terrorism designations on October 2, 2026. These actions target individuals and entities identified as supporting terrorist activities globally.

The designations aim to disrupt the financial networks of terrorist organizations by freezing assets and prohibiting transactions with U.S. persons. This is part of the U.S. government's ongoing efforts to combat international terrorism.

Further details regarding the specific individuals and entities designated were not immediately provided. Financial institutions and other regulated entities are advised to screen their transactions and customer bases against OFAC's updated Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) List.

articles.headline: EU Adopts New Sanctions Package Against Russia, Targeting Sanctions Evasion
body: The Council of the European Union adopted additional restrictive measures against three individuals and nine entities on October 15, 2026, targeting those involved in the import of sanctioned goods to Russia and the circumvention of EU sanctions related to oil and financial transactions. This marks a significant escalation in the EU's efforts to counter sanctions evasion.

The new listings include Russian cargo delivery companies like Movers Group LLC and LLC DT Inier, along with its majority shareholder Ivanna Savchuk, for their roles in parallel imports and decentralized sanctions circumvention schemes. Turkish trade companies Begler Tekstil Insaat Elektronik Ve Dis Ticaret Ltd and Medse Group LLC, operating global networks, were also sanctioned.

Furthermore, the EU targeted United Stream LLC, a Russian financial services company, and its founder Svetlana Gumenyuk, for facilitating the import of sanctioned EU goods. Sanctions were also imposed on entities based in the United Arab Emirates, India, and the Seychelles—Dis Logistics DMCC, Vigor Marine Services LLP, and Shiva Shipping Ltd.—for their involvement in the 'shadow fleet' ecosystem, alongside trading intermediary Hurus Trade FZE, for circumvention of oil-related EU sanctions.
articles.source: Council of the European Union / The Sofia Globe

articles.headline: EU Imposes Record Sanctions on Russia's Military-Industrial Complex and DPRK Over WMD Programs
body: The Council of the European Union adopted additional restrictive measures on October 12, 2026, against 1,569 individuals and entities within Russia's military and industrial complex, marking the largest single set of listings ever approved by the EU. This action brings the total number of listings under the Russia sanctions regime to almost 4,600.

The sanctions specifically target mid-level suppliers that form the core of the Russian military industry, generating substantial annual turnover and employing a significant workforce. These companies are identified as suppliers of key components for Russia's advanced weapons systems, including missiles, UAVs, and aircraft.

Concurrently, the EU added three individuals and four entities to its autonomous sanctions list on the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK). These designations are in response to their involvement in supporting, promoting, or facilitating activities that contribute to the DPRK's nuclear weapons, ballistic missile, or other weapons of mass destruction programs, as well as for violating and evading United Nations sanctions. The new listings also target activities linked to the growing military and economic cooperation between the DPRK and Russia.
articles.source: Council of the European Union / Hill Dickinson / Morgan Lewis

articles.headline: President Trump Waives Key Sanctions from Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act
body: President Donald Trump signed an executive order on October 16, 2026, waiving substantial additional sanctions and trade restrictions established under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026. This move, which came two days before the act was set to take effect, has drawn criticism from members of Congress.

The waived measures included an additional 500% tariff on Russian goods and 100% tariffs on imports from countries meeting specified criteria for Russian energy purchases or sanctions evasion. The executive order also suspended new restrictions concerning Russian financial institutions, investment, energy transactions, and sovereign debt.

While the broader U.S. sanctions regime against Russia remains in place, this waiver suspends prospective American tariff pressure on major purchasers of Russian energy, such as China and India, and other significant importers like Turkey. The decision has been linked to a deal for Russian diesel fuel, which is in short supply globally.
articles.source: The White House / Reuters / The Guardian

articles.headline: Bank of America Fined Over $11.6 Million by OFAC for Sanctions Violations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a civil penalty of $11,662,930 against Bank of America, N.A. on October 13, 2026. This significant fine is part of broader enforcement actions taken by the U.S. Department of the Treasury against the bank for violations of anti-money laundering and sanctions laws.

The penalty stems from Bank of America's failure to mitigate and report priority national security risks, including those related to Chinese Money Laundering Networks and illicit finance along the southwest border. This action underscores OFAC's commitment to holding financial institutions accountable for sanctions compliance.

This OFAC penalty is in addition to a $750 million civil money penalty imposed by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) and a $1.2 billion penalty assessed by the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) for deficient BSA/AML compliance programs. The combined actions represent a substantial enforcement effort by U.S. regulators.

articles.headline: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics Pays $175,015 OFAC Civil Penalty
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a civil penalty of $175,015 against Pegasus Worldwide Logistics on October 9, 2026. This penalty is the result of a settlement agreement between OFAC and the logistics company for apparent violations of U.S. sanctions regulations.

While the specific details of the violations were not immediately disclosed in the penalty announcement, such actions typically involve transactions or dealings with sanctioned countries, entities, or individuals. OFAC continues to emphasize the importance of robust compliance programs for all businesses, including those in the logistics sector.

This enforcement action serves as a reminder to companies operating internationally of their obligations to adhere to U.S. sanctions laws and implement effective internal controls to prevent prohibited transactions.

articles.headline: Individual Fined Over $1.4 Million by OFAC for Sanctions Violations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a civil penalty of $1,427,230 against an individual on September 10, 2026. This significant fine highlights OFAC's commitment to enforcing sanctions regulations against individuals as well as corporate entities.

Details surrounding the specific violations committed by the individual were not immediately made public, but such penalties typically arise from unauthorized transactions with sanctioned jurisdictions, entities, or persons. Individuals are expected to comply with U.S. sanctions laws, and ignorance of the law is generally not a defense.

This enforcement action serves as a strong deterrent and a reminder that individuals, like corporations, are subject to substantial penalties for breaches of OFAC regulations. It underscores the importance of due diligence and adherence to sanctions compliance for all U.S. persons and those subject to U.S. jurisdiction.

articles.headline: Rice Lake Weighing Systems, Inc. Pays $60,764 OFAC Civil Penalty
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a civil penalty of $60,764 against Rice Lake Weighing Systems, Inc. on August 12, 2026. This penalty is the result of a settlement agreement with the company for apparent violations of U.S. sanctions regulations.

While the specific nature of the violations was not detailed in the public announcement, OFAC enforcement actions against companies often relate to dealings with sanctioned countries or individuals. Companies are expected to implement and maintain robust sanctions compliance programs to prevent such violations.
This action serves as a reminder to businesses of all sizes about the importance of adhering to U.S. sanctions laws and the potential financial consequences of non-compliance.

articles.headline: Houthi Attacks Escalate Yemen Conflict, Threaten Saudi Civilian Infrastructure
body: The conflict between Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi movement has sharply escalated, with repeated Houthi attacks on Saudi airports carrying the conflict directly into Saudi civilian infrastructure. A missile attack on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport on October 10 killed 13 people and injured over 300, followed by another strike on October 11 that killed one person and injured 11.

Saudi authorities also confirmed an attack on King Fahd International Airport in Dammam. These incidents follow a Saudi-backed military offensive against Houthi forces in Yemen, marking a significant intensification of the conflict.

The attacks demonstrate the Houthis' ability to impose substantial economic and political costs, and Washington is reportedly considering direct participation in Saudi military operations against the Houthis, which would represent a further widening of the Yemen confrontation. Meanwhile, negotiations over reopening the Strait of Hormuz remain unresolved, with Iranian attacks on commercial tankers expanding beyond the strait into the wider Persian Gulf.

articles.headline: OCC Imposes Record $750 Million Penalty on Bank of America for BSA/AML Deficiencies
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) announced a historic $750 million civil money penalty against Bank of America, N.A., on October 13, 2026, for widespread violations of the Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) and its implementing regulations. This represents the largest civil money penalty in OCC history.

The OCC found that Bank of America's BSA/AML compliance program was deficient and ineffective, with its transaction monitoring system failing to properly monitor trillions of dollars in transactions. This resulted in the bank filing a large number of late suspicious activity reports (SARs) involving billions of dollars, many of which had indicia of money laundering.

This action was taken in coordination with the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN), which assessed a separate $1.2 billion fine against the bank, crediting the OCC's penalty. The OCC emphasized that the bank's poor response to its longstanding BSA deficiencies was unacceptable, warranting swift and significant action.
articles.source: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency

articles.headline: OCC Releases Report on 'Debanking' Practices by Large Banks, Citing Reputational Risk Policies
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) released a report on October 14, 2026, detailing alleged 'debanking' practices by the nine largest U.S. banks, where customers were denied or limited financial services due to their political beliefs or business activities. The report, titled 'Guaranteeing Fair Banking for All Americans,' was directed by President Trump's executive order issued last year.

The OCC found multiple examples of public and nonpublic policies restricting access to financial services for certain industry sectors, including oil and gas exploration, coal mining, firearms manufacturing, and digital asset activities. The agency attributed much of the blame to 'inexact' reputational risk policies, which infused the value judgments of stakeholders into banks' business decisions.

The OCC, along with the FDIC and Federal Reserve, has taken steps to remove reputational risk from bank supervision, including a final rule earlier this year banning its use by supervisors. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) also announced an initiative to investigate whether banks complied with federal consumer financial laws in these practices.
articles.source: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency / ABA Banking Journal

articles.headline: OCC Assesses $350 Million Civil Money Penalty Against American Express

articles.headline: Commerce Department Amends GlobalFoundries CHIPS Award, Reallocates $955 Million for Advanced Semiconductor Investments
body: The Department of Commerce's CHIPS Program Office announced an agreement with GlobalFoundries on October 14, 2026, to amend its existing award and reallocate up to $955 million in incentives under the CHIPS and Science Act. This amendment will increase the portion of the award allocated to GlobalFoundries' modernization and expansion of its semiconductor manufacturing facilities in Malta, NY, and Burlington, VT.

As part of this agreement, GlobalFoundries has committed to expanding its capital investment in these facilities to $5 billion. The total amount of the existing CHIPS Program award will not be increased, but the reallocation aims to accelerate investments in critical technologies such as silicon photonics, silicon-germanium, and the first U.S.-based source of silicon interposers supporting advanced packaging technologies.

This initiative is part of a broader U.S.-Japan strategic investment, enabled by President Donald J. Trump's trade and investment agreement with Japan, which unlocks up to $21 billion in funding to accelerate trusted semiconductor manufacturing in the United States, strengthen critical supply chains, and support growing demand across various markets. Bill Frauenhofer, Executive Director for Semiconductor Innovation and Investment at the Department of Commerce, emphasized the strategic expansion of the U.S. semiconductor ecosystem through the CHIPS Act, trade agreements, and R&D investments.

articles.headline: Revisions to the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) revises the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing two addresses associated with Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. from the Entity List under the destination of China, People's Republic of (China). This determination follows the removal from the Entity List of Arrow China Electronics Trading Co., Ltd., and the removal of six aliases for Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. in November 2025.

articles.headline: Removal From the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing one entity from the Entity List under the destination of Turkey.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.

articles.headline: Enhanced Favorable Treatment for the United Arab Emirates Under the Export Administration Regulations
body: In this final rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to provide enhanced favorable treatment for the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Specifically, BIS is removing the UAE from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 and adding the UAE to Country Group A:5. More license exceptions will now be available, including Strategic Trade Authorization (STA) for the UAE Government and approved commercial entities in the UAE. STA will authorize the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) of military items; certain commercial satellites and spacecraft; and dual-use items useful in, inter alia, oil and gas production, desalination, and civil nuclear power generation. The UAE Government and approved commercial entities will also have license-free access to advanced computing items, consistent with the May 2025 U.S.-UAE Artificial Intelligence Cooperation framework, without compromising U.S. digital infrastructure buildout.
